sections.title: Task 2 Essays
sections.intro:
Five skeletons (one per essay type) + one full band-9 essay each.

Learn the skeleton first, then the essay. Braces = chunk to memorise. [X] = fill in.

Time plan: 5 min plan · 30 min write · 5 min check. Aim 270–300 words.

items.title: Skeleton: Opinion (agree / disagree)
items.q: Give the 4-paragraph skeleton for "To what extent do you agree or disagree?"
items.tip: Same opinion from intro to conclusion. Never "partly agree" unless you can explain exactly which part.
items.html:
Intro: It is often argued that [paraphrase the statement]. I agree with this view to a large extent, because [reason 1] and [reason 2].

Body 1: The main reason I support this view is that [reason 1]. This is because [explain]. For example, [specific example]. As a result, [consequence].

Body 2: A further reason is that [reason 2]. [explain + example]. Admittedly, [other side], but this does not outweigh [your point].

Conclusion: In conclusion, I firmly believe that [restate opinion]. If [action], [benefit].

items.title: Sample: Opinion — free university
items.q: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
items.tip: Pattern: intro gives opinion + 2 reasons → each body = 1 reason → concession inside body 2.
items.html:
It is often argued that tertiary education should be funded entirely by the state so that every student can attend university free of charge. While I accept that this would widen access to higher education, I disagree with making it free for everyone, as it would place an unsustainable burden on public finances and benefit those who need help least.

The main reason I oppose universal free tuition is the cost. Degrees are expensive to deliver, and if governments paid every student's fees, the money would have to come from higher taxes or cuts to services such as healthcare and primary schools. This is particularly unfair because many taxpayers never attend university themselves, so they would be subsidising the future earnings of a relatively privileged group. Graduates typically earn considerably more over their lifetimes than non-graduates, which makes it reasonable to expect them to contribute to the cost of their own education.

A further reason is that free tuition does not necessarily help the poorest students. The real barrier for low-income families is often living costs rather than fees. A more effective policy would be means-tested grants and loans, which target support at those who would otherwise be unable to study. Admittedly, free education sends a powerful message that learning is a right rather than a privilege, but this symbolic benefit does not outweigh the practical drawbacks.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that university should not be free for all. Instead, governments should direct funding towards disadvantaged students, ensuring that talent rather than wealth determines who receives a degree.

items.title: Skeleton: Discuss both views
items.q: Give the skeleton for "Discuss both views and give your own opinion."
items.tip: Equal space to both views. Your opinion appears in the intro AND conclusion (and can open body 2).
items.html:
Intro: There is an ongoing debate as to whether [topic]. While some argue that [view A], others believe that [view B]. In my view, [your side].

Body 1: On the one hand, those who favour [view A] point out that [reason + example].

Body 2: On the other hand, I side with those who believe [view B], mainly because [reason + example].

Conclusion: In conclusion, although [view A] has some merit, I am convinced that [view B].

items.title: Sample: Discussion — early school start
items.q: Some people think children should start formal education at a very early age, while others believe they should not begin school until they are older. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.html:
There is an ongoing debate as to whether children benefit from starting school when they are very young. While some argue that an early start gives children a head start academically, others believe that young children should spend their first years learning through play. In my view, the second approach is wiser.

On the one hand, those who favour early schooling point out that young children absorb information remarkably quickly. Starting reading and arithmetic at three or four, they argue, allows pupils to build a strong foundation before more demanding subjects begin. Early schooling can also be valuable for children from disadvantaged homes, who may not receive much intellectual stimulation outside the classroom.

On the other hand, I side with those who believe formal lessons should wait, mainly because play is not a waste of time for young children. Through unstructured play they develop language, creativity and the ability to cooperate, which are the building blocks of later learning. Finland, whose pupils do not begin formal schooling until the age of seven, consistently performs well in international rankings, suggesting that a late start does no lasting harm. In contrast, pushing toddlers to sit still and complete worksheets may put them off learning before they have had a chance to enjoy it.

In conclusion, although an early start has some merit, particularly for children who lack support at home, I am convinced that formal education should begin later. The priority for young children should be curiosity and social skills, not test results.

items.title: Skeleton: Advantages outweigh disadvantages?
items.q: Give the skeleton for "Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?"
items.tip: The question asks for a verdict — say which side wins in the intro. Give the losing side 1 short paragraph.
items.html:
Intro: [paraphrase]. Although this trend has certain drawbacks, I believe the benefits are far more significant.

Body 1 (weaker side): Admittedly, there are some disadvantages to [X]. The most obvious is that [drawback + example].

Body 2 (stronger side): However, these drawbacks are outweighed by [benefit 1]. Moreover, [benefit 2 + example].

Conclusion: Overall, while [X] is not without its problems, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

items.title: Sample: Adv/Dis — working from home
items.q: More and more people now work from home instead of travelling to an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
items.html:
In recent years, a growing number of employees have begun working from home rather than commuting to an office. Although this trend has certain drawbacks, I believe the benefits are far more significant.

Admittedly, there are some disadvantages to remote working. The most obvious is that employees may feel isolated, as they miss out on the informal conversations that take place in a shared workplace. These interactions are not trivial: they help new staff learn from experienced colleagues and often spark new ideas. In addition, some people find it difficult to draw a clear line between work and home life, which can lead to longer working hours and stress.

However, these drawbacks are outweighed by the advantages. Firstly, working from home eliminates the daily commute, which in large cities can take two hours or more. This time can be spent with family, exercising or resting, which improves employees' well-being and, in turn, their productivity. Moreover, remote work benefits society as a whole. Fewer cars on the road means less congestion and lower carbon emissions, while companies can recruit talented people who live far from major cities. Many firms that adopted flexible working during the pandemic have found that output remained stable or even rose.

Overall, while working from home is not without its problems, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages. The challenge for employers is to provide opportunities for regular face-to-face contact, so that staff enjoy flexibility without losing a sense of belonging.

items.title: Skeleton: Causes / Problems + Solutions
items.q: Give the skeleton for "What are the causes (problems) and what solutions can you suggest?"
items.tip: Each solution must match a cause. Be specific: WHO should do WHAT.
items.html:
Intro: [paraphrase]. This essay will examine the main causes of this issue and suggest some practical solutions.

Body 1: The primary cause of [problem] is [cause 1]. [explain + example]. Another contributing factor is [cause 2].

Body 2: There are several measures that could be taken to address this. First and foremost, governments should [solution 1]. In addition, [solution 2], which would [result].

Conclusion: In summary, [problem] stems largely from [causes]. However, it could be tackled if [solutions].

items.title: Sample: Causes/Solutions — traffic congestion
items.q: Traffic congestion is becoming a serious problem in many cities. What are the causes of this problem, and what solutions can you suggest?
items.html:
Traffic jams have become a daily reality in cities across the world, wasting time and polluting the air. This essay will examine the main causes of this issue and suggest some practical solutions.

The primary cause of congestion is the sheer number of private vehicles on the road. As incomes rise in developing countries, owning a car has become both affordable and a symbol of status, and millions of new drivers join the roads each year. Another contributing factor is inadequate public transport. Where buses are slow and unreliable and train networks do not reach the suburbs, residents have little choice but to drive. Finally, poor urban planning means that many people live far from their workplaces, so commuting distances have grown steadily.

There are several measures that could be taken to address this. First and foremost, governments should invest heavily in public transport, creating fast, frequent and affordable services that are a genuine alternative to the car. Bus lanes and metro systems, such as those built in Bogotá and Seoul, have significantly reduced journey times. In addition, authorities could introduce congestion charges, which make drivers pay to enter the city centre at peak times; London's scheme cut traffic in the charging zone considerably. In the longer term, planners should build mixed-use neighbourhoods where homes, offices and shops are close together, reducing the need to travel at all.

In summary, congestion stems largely from rising car ownership and weak alternatives. However, it could be tackled if governments made public transport more attractive and discouraged unnecessary driving.

items.title: Skeleton: Two-part question
items.q: Give the skeleton for a two-part question (e.g. "Why is this? Is it positive or negative?")
items.tip: Answer BOTH questions in the intro, one body paragraph each. Most common mistake: forgetting part 2.
items.html:
Intro: [paraphrase]. This is largely due to [reason], and I believe it is a [positive/negative] development overall.

Body 1 (question 1): There are several reasons for this trend. The most significant is that [reason 1]. Furthermore, [reason 2 + example].

Body 2 (question 2): In my view, this is a [positive] development because [reason + example]. That said, [small reservation].

Conclusion: To conclude, [answer 1] and [answer 2].

items.title: Sample: Two-part — living alone
items.q: In many countries, more and more people are choosing to live alone. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development?
items.html:
In many parts of the world, single-person households are becoming increasingly common. This is largely due to economic and social change, and I believe it is a broadly positive development, although it carries some risks.

There are several reasons for this trend. The most significant is greater financial independence. As more people, particularly women, enter well-paid careers, they no longer need to share a home in order to afford one. Furthermore, social attitudes have shifted: people now marry later or not at all, and living alone is no longer seen as a sign of failure but as a deliberate lifestyle choice. Longer life expectancy also plays a part, since many elderly people continue to live independently after the death of a partner.

In my view, this is a positive development because it reflects greater personal freedom. Living alone allows people to organise their time as they wish, to focus on their careers and to develop self-reliance. It is also a sign that societies are wealthy enough to offer people genuine choices. That said, the risk of loneliness should not be ignored, especially among older people, whose health can suffer when they have little daily contact with others. Communities and local authorities therefore have a role to play in providing social activities and support.

To conclude, the rise in solo living is driven mainly by financial independence and changing attitudes, and on balance it is a welcome change, provided that those who live alone do not become isolated.

sections.title: Task 2 Topic Bank
sections.intro:
14 topics that cover most Task 2 questions (and Speaking Part 3).

Each topic: an Ideas card (common question + ready arguments with examples) and a Collocations card.

Ideas are reusable: the same argument works for many questions on that topic.

items.title: Education — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Should schools teach practical life skills (e.g. managing money) instead of academic subjects?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: online vs classroom learning · single-sex schools · should university be free · are exams the best way to assess students · teachers vs technology.
items.html:
• FOR practical skills: many school-leavers lack basic financial literacy, e.g. they take on debts they do not understand.
  • FOR: employers complain that graduates are ill-equipped for the workplace; teamwork and communication can be taught.
  • FOR academic: core subjects develop critical thinking, which transfers to every area of life.
  • FOR academic: practical skills are better learnt at home or on the job; schools have limited time.

items.title: Education — collocations
items.html:
• Many school-leavers choose to pursue higher education abroad.
  • Rote learning produces students who can repeat facts but cannot apply them.
  • Arts and sport are essential for a well-rounded education.
  • Students acquire knowledge and skills that prepare them for employment.
  • Children from poor families are more likely to drop out of school.
  • In a fast-changing economy, lifelong learning is no longer optional.
  • Parental involvement is strongly linked to academic achievement.
  • Internships bridge the gap between theory and practice.

items.title: Technology — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Has technology made our lives more complicated or easier?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: children and screens · AI replacing jobs · online friendships · cashless society · does technology isolate people.
items.html:
• EASIER: everyday tasks such as banking and shopping can be done in a matter of minutes on a phone.
  • EASIER: video calls allow families to stay in touch across continents.
  • HARDER: constant notifications blur the boundary between work and leisure.
  • HARDER: people must protect themselves from scams and data breaches, which older users find confusing.

items.title: Technology — collocations
items.html:
• Hospitals now use cutting-edge technology to detect cancer early.
  • We have become increasingly reliant on smartphones for navigation.
  • Social media is a double-edged sword: it connects and divides.
  • Children need face-to-face interaction to develop social skills.
  • Technological advances have transformed the way we work.
  • Doctors recommend limiting children's screen time to an hour a day.
  • Automation may render many routine jobs obsolete.
  • Some see facial recognition cameras as an invasion of privacy.

items.title: Environment — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Is climate change the responsibility of governments or individuals?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: plastic waste · should flying be taxed · protecting endangered species · renewable energy · fast fashion · is it too late to act.
items.html:
• GOVERNMENTS: only states can impose legally binding targets on industry, e.g. emissions limits for factories.
  • GOVERNMENTS: large projects like renewable grids require enormous investment.
  • INDIVIDUALS: consumer choices drive demand; if people buy fewer cars and less meat, companies adapt.
  • INDIVIDUALS: governments in democracies follow public opinion; citizens must push for change.

items.title: Environment — collocations
items.html:
• Cycling to work is a simple way to reduce our carbon footprint.
  • Countries should switch to renewable energy sources such as wind and solar.
  • Rising sea levels pose a serious threat to coastal cities.
  • Deforestation destroys the natural habitats of countless species.
  • Some scientists warn that pollution may cause irreversible damage to the oceans.
  • Several countries have banned single-use plastics such as straws.
  • Governments must take drastic measures to cut emissions.
  • Overconsumption leads to the depletion of natural resources.

items.title: Health — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Should governments tax unhealthy food (e.g. sugary drinks) to fight obesity?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: prevention vs treatment · public vs private healthcare · sport in schools · why people are less active · free healthcare for all.
items.html:
• FOR: taxes change consumer behaviour; the UK sugar tax led companies to cut sugar in drinks.
  • FOR: the revenue can fund public health campaigns or school sport.
  • AGAINST: such taxes hit low-income families hardest, as they spend more of their income on food.
  • AGAINST: obesity has many causes; education is more effective than punishment.

items.title: Health — collocations
items.html:
• Office workers often lead a sedentary lifestyle.
  • Diets high in sugar can lead to obesity.
  • Since prevention is better than cure, funding should go to education.
  • An ageing population puts a strain on the healthcare system.
  • Life expectancy has risen thanks to medical advances.
  • Regular exercise improves mental well-being as well as fitness.
  • Processed food is cheap but often full of salt and fat.
  • Campaigns can raise awareness of the dangers of smoking.

items.title: Crime & punishment — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Is prison the best way to reduce crime, or are education and rehabilitation better?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: why young people commit crime · longer sentences · community service · should police carry guns · CCTV everywhere.
items.html:
• PRISON: it protects the public from dangerous offenders and acts as a deterrent.
  • PRISON: victims need to see that justice has been done.
  • REHABILITATION: prisons often act as breeding grounds for crime; inmates learn from other criminals.
  • REHABILITATION: Norway's focus on education and job training gives it one of the lowest reoffending rates in the world.

items.title: Crime & punishment — collocations
items.html:
• Most young people who commit a crime come from troubled backgrounds.
  • Heavy fines act as a deterrent to dangerous driving.
  • Ex-prisoners without jobs are far more likely to reoffend.
  • He served a five-year sentence for fraud.
  • Minor offenders could do community service instead of going to prison.
  • Poverty and lack of education are the root causes of crime.
  • Training helps prisoners reintegrate into society after release.
  • Most law-abiding citizens support stronger policing.

items.title: Work — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Is job satisfaction more important than a high salary?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: one job for life vs changing jobs · four-day week · gap year · work-life balance · should young people be paid less.
items.html:
• SATISFACTION: people spend a third of their lives at work; misery at work affects health and family.
  • SATISFACTION: motivated staff are more productive, so it benefits employers too.
  • SALARY: for many, a high income is a necessity rather than a luxury, e.g. to pay rent or support parents.
  • SALARY: money provides security and the freedom to pursue interests outside work.

items.title: Work — collocations
items.html:
• Many people value job satisfaction more than a large salary.
  • A four-day week could improve work-life balance.
  • Ambitious graduates want to climb the career ladder quickly.
  • Contract workers have little job security.
  • Graduates face a highly competitive job market.
  • Employees who work long hours without breaks often burn out.
  • Part-time jobs let students gain hands-on experience.
  • The unemployment rate among young people remains stubbornly high.

items.title: Government spending — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Should governments spend money on the arts (museums, theatre) when there are more urgent needs?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: space exploration vs problems on Earth · public transport vs roads · foreign aid · should healthcare be free · funding sport.
items.html:
• ARTS: culture defines a nation's identity and attracts tourists, who bring money.
  • ARTS: art spending is a tiny fraction of the national budget; cutting it would not fix hospitals.
  • URGENT NEEDS: while people lack basic healthcare, spending on galleries is hard to justify.
  • URGENT NEEDS: the arts can be funded by private sponsors and ticket sales.

items.title: Government spending — collocations
items.html:
• The government should allocate more funds to rural schools.
  • Taxpayers' money must be spent responsibly.
  • Healthcare should be a top priority for any government.
  • Cuts to public services hit the poorest hardest.
  • Critics regard space programmes as a waste of resources.
  • Investing in research is in the national interest.
  • Large infrastructure projects create thousands of jobs.
  • The welfare state protects people who lose their jobs.

items.title: Globalisation & culture — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Is globalisation causing the loss of local cultures and traditions?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: should everyone learn English · international tourism and culture · disappearing languages · global brands.
items.html:
• YES: young people adopt Western fashions and fast food, while traditional crafts and festivals decline.
  • YES: of about 7,000 languages, many are on the verge of extinction.
  • NO: globalisation helps traditions reach a global audience, e.g. Korean music and Indian cuisine.
  • NO: cultures have always evolved through contact with others; change is not loss.

items.title: Globalisation & culture — collocations
items.html:
• Language is central to a people's cultural identity.
  • Global brands threaten cultural diversity.
  • Festivals help communities preserve traditions.
  • The internet has turned the world into a global village.
  • Multinational corporations dominate many local markets.
  • Some fear a single homogenous culture will replace local ones.
  • Student exchanges encourage cultural exchange and tolerance.
  • Family recipes are passed down from generation to generation.

items.title: Media & advertising — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Should advertising aimed at children be banned?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: is news trustworthy · social media influencers · online news vs newspapers · celebrities as role models · fake news.
items.html:
• BAN: children cannot distinguish adverts from entertainment and are easily manipulated.
  • BAN: junk-food adverts contribute to childhood obesity.
  • NO BAN: parents, not governments, should take responsibility for what children watch.
  • NO BAN: advertising funds free children's content; a ban could reduce quality programmes.

items.title: Media & advertising — collocations
items.html:
• The mass media shapes public opinion.
  • Toy adverts have children as their target audience.
  • Social media can spread misinformation within hours.
  • Not every website is a reliable source of information.
  • Adverts persuade people to buy things they do not need.
  • Paparazzi often invade people's privacy.
  • Freedom of the press is vital in a democracy.
  • A single video can go viral overnight.

items.title: Family & children — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Are parents or schools more responsible for teaching children how to behave?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: working mothers · grandparents raising children · children and pocket money · smaller families · children growing up too fast.
items.html:
• PARENTS: children learn by example, and they spend most of their early years at home.
  • PARENTS: values like honesty are rooted in family life.
  • SCHOOLS: teachers show children how to cooperate with people from different backgrounds.
  • SCHOOLS: some children do not receive guidance at home; school is their only role model.

items.title: Family & children — collocations
items.html:
• Bringing up children is more expensive than ever.
  • Parents are a child's first role model.
  • The nuclear family has replaced the extended family in many cities.
  • Busy parents struggle to spend quality time with their children.
  • Schools can help instil values such as respect.
  • Giving children everything they want can spoil them.
  • Technology has widened the generation gap.
  • Single-parent families often need extra financial support.

items.title: Cities & transport — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Should cities ban private cars from their centres?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: urbanisation problems · high-rise living · rural vs city life · free public transport · building new roads.
items.html:
• BAN: cleaner air and quieter streets make city centres more liveable, e.g. Oslo's car-free centre.
  • BAN: it frees up space for cycle lanes, parks and cafés.
  • AGAINST: the elderly and disabled depend on cars for access.
  • AGAINST: shops may lose customers, damaging the local economy.

items.title: Cities & transport — collocations
items.html:
• Urban sprawl swallows farmland around big cities.
  • Traffic congestion costs the economy billions.
  • An efficient public transport network reduces car use.
  • Rural-urban migration is driven by the search for jobs.
  • The cost of living in capital cities is rising sharply.
  • Overcrowded housing harms children's health.
  • Pedestrianised zones make shopping more pleasant.
  • Air pollution causes millions of early deaths each year.

items.title: Tourism — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Does international tourism do more harm than good?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: overtourism · should historic sites charge tourists more · space tourism · travel broadens the mind.
items.html:
• GOOD: tourism creates jobs and brings foreign currency, especially in poorer regions.
  • GOOD: travel broadens the mind and reduces prejudice.
  • HARM: overtourism drives up housing costs for locals, e.g. in Venice and Barcelona.
  • HARM: mass tourism can damage fragile ecosystems such as coral reefs.

items.title: Tourism — collocations
items.html:
• The tourism industry employs millions worldwide.
  • Popular tourist attractions are crowded in summer.
  • Mass tourism is damaging historic city centres.
  • Festivals boost the local economy.
  • Some travellers prefer places off the beaten track.
  • Eco-friendly tourism protects the environment.
  • Travelling abroad broadens one's horizons.
  • Historical landmarks need protection from crowds.

items.title: Science & space — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Is space exploration a waste of money when there are problems on Earth?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: animal testing · genetic engineering · should science be funded by companies · AI research.
items.html:
• WORTH IT: space research has produced everyday technologies such as GPS and weather satellites.
  • WORTH IT: monitoring Earth from space helps us understand climate change.
  • WASTE: billions could lift millions out of poverty instead.
  • WASTE: private companies can now take on the financial risk instead of governments.

items.title: Science & space — collocations
items.html:
• The vaccine was a major scientific breakthrough.
  • Universities conduct research funded by the state.
  • Space missions push the boundaries of human knowledge.
  • Genetic engineering raises serious ethical concerns.
  • Research must have practical applications.
  • In the long run, the investment pays for itself.
  • Medical research helps cure diseases.
  • Space programmes created many spin-off technologies.

items.title: Arts, sport & leisure — ideas
items.q: Common question: "Are professional sportspeople paid too much?" — give 2 ideas each side.
items.tip: Also asked: arts at school · should museums be free · sport for children · computer games · watching vs playing sport.
items.html:
• TOO MUCH: footballers earn more in a week than nurses earn in a year, which seems unfair.
  • TOO MUCH: huge salaries send the wrong message to young people about what society values.
  • FAIR: careers are short and require years of dedication; injury can end them overnight.
  • FAIR: salaries reflect the revenue they generate from tickets and TV rights.

items.title: Arts, sport & leisure — collocations
items.html:
• Top athletes are a source of inspiration for children.
  • Finishing a marathon gives you a real sense of achievement.
  • Team sports build team spirit.
  • Art is a form of creative expression.
  • People now have more choice of leisure activities.
  • Many people swim to keep fit.
  • Visiting galleries teaches children to appreciate art.
  • High salaries are a well-deserved reward for talent.

sections.title: Task 1 Academic
sections.intro:
Formula: Intro (paraphrase) → Overview (2 main features, no numbers) → Body 1 → Body 2. No conclusion, no opinion.

Aim 170–190 words in 20 minutes. The overview is the single most important sentence for band 7+.

items.title: Template: any chart
items.q: Say the 4-paragraph Task 1 template.
items.tip: Paraphrase: shows → illustrates / compares / gives information about · number of → how many · percentage → proportion.
items.html:
Intro: […] i…">The [line graph] illustrates [what] in [place] between [year] and [year].

Overview: Overall, it is clear that [biggest trend], while [second key feature].

Body 1: Looking at the details, [group A] stood at [x] in [year], before rising steadily to [y] by [year].

Body 2: By contrast, [group B] … Meanwhile, [group C] remained relatively stable at around [z].

items.title: Template: process & map
items.q: Say the intro + overview templates for a process diagram and for a map.
items.tip: Process → present simple passive (is heated, is collected). Map → past simple passive / present perfect (was built, has been replaced).
items.html:
Process intro: The diagram illustrates the process by which [X] is produced.

Process overview: Overall, there are [eight] main stages in the process, beginning with [A] and ending with [B].

Process body: In the first stage, … Following this, … Once [X] has been [dried], … Finally, …

Map intro: The maps compare [the town of X] in [year] and [year].

Map overview: Overall, the area became far more [urbanised], with [farmland] being replaced by [housing].

Map body: To the north of [X], [a park] was built … The woodland in the east was cleared to make way for …

items.title: Sample: Line graph — internet access
items.q: The line graph shows the percentage of households with internet access in three countries, 2000–2020. (A: 40% → 95% · B: 10% → 50% in 2010 → 80% · C: 5% → 15% in 2010 → 35%)
items.html:
The line graph illustrates the proportion of households that had internet access in three countries, labelled A, B and C, between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, it is clear that internet access increased in all three countries over the period, with Country A remaining the most connected throughout, while Country C lagged considerably behind the others.

In 2000, 40% of homes in Country A were online, four times the figure for Country B (10%). Access in Country A rose steadily, reaching almost every household (95%) by 2020. Country B saw the most dramatic growth: its figure climbed sharply to 50% in 2010 and continued upwards to 80% at the end of the period.

Country C, by contrast, started from a very low base of just 5%. Growth was slow in the first decade, with the proportion only reaching 15% by 2010. However, the rate of increase accelerated in the second half of the period, and by 2020 just over a third of households (35%) had access, which was still less than half the level of Country A.

items.title: Sample: Bar chart — transport to work
items.q: The bar chart compares how people travelled to work in a city in 1990 and 2020 (Car 45% → 30% · Bus 25% → 20% · Bicycle 5% → 25% · Walking 25% → 25%).
items.html:
The bar chart compares the methods of transport that commuters in a city used to get to work in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the car remained the most popular means of transport, although its share fell, while cycling experienced the most significant growth over the thirty-year period.

In 1990, almost half of all commuters (45%) travelled by car, compared with a quarter who took the bus and the same proportion who walked. Cycling was by far the least common option, accounting for just 5% of journeys.

By 2020, the picture had changed considerably. The proportion of people driving to work dropped by a third to 30%, and bus use also declined slightly, to 20%. In contrast, the figure for cycling rose fivefold, to 25%, making the bicycle as popular as walking, which was the only method of transport to remain unchanged at 25%.

items.title: Sample: Pie charts — household spending
items.q: Two pie charts show average household spending in a country in 1980 and 2020 (Food 40% → 20% · Housing 20% → 35% · Transport 15% → 15% · Leisure 10% → 20% · Other 15% → 10%).
items.html:
The pie charts compare how the average household in a particular country divided its budget in 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the most notable change was the shift from spending on food to spending on housing, which became the largest category of expenditure by 2020.

In 1980, food accounted for the largest share of household spending, at 40%, twice as much as housing (20%). Transport made up 15% of the budget, while leisure represented just one tenth. The remaining 15% went on other items.

Forty years later, the proportion spent on food had halved to 20%. Housing, by contrast, rose to over a third of the total (35%), and spending on leisure also doubled, to 20%. Transport was the only category to remain constant, at 15%, while other costs fell slightly to 10%.

items.title: Sample: Table — university students
items.q: The table shows the number of international students (thousands) in four countries in 2010 and 2020 (USA 690 → 1,000 · UK 400 → 550 · Australia 230 → 460 · Canada 100 → 500).
items.html:
The table gives information about the number of international students in four countries in 2010 and 2020.

Overall, all four countries attracted more overseas students over the decade, and while the USA remained the leading destination, Canada saw by far the fastest rate of growth.

In 2010, the USA hosted 690,000 international students, considerably more than the UK, with 400,000. Australia and Canada had much smaller numbers, at 230,000 and 100,000 respectively.

By 2020, the figure for the USA had risen to one million, and the UK saw a more modest increase to 550,000. Australia's number doubled to 460,000. The most striking change, however, was in Canada, where the number of overseas students increased fivefold to 500,000, overtaking Australia and coming close to the UK.

items.title: Sample: Process — recycling glass bottles
items.q: The diagram shows how glass bottles are recycled (collection → transport to plant → cleaning → sorting by colour → crushing → melting with sand → moulding into new bottles → delivered to shops).
items.html:
The diagram illustrates the process by which used glass bottles are recycled into new ones.

Overall, there are eight stages in the process, beginning with the collection of used bottles and ending with the delivery of new bottles to shops.

In the first stage, used bottles are collected from recycling bins and transported by lorry to a recycling plant. There, they are thoroughly cleaned to remove labels and dirt. Following this, the bottles are sorted according to colour, after which they are crushed into small pieces.

In the next step, the crushed glass is melted in a furnace together with sand and other raw materials. The liquid glass is then poured into moulds and shaped into new bottles. Finally, the new bottles are delivered to shops and supermarkets, where they are filled and sold, and the cycle begins again.

items.title: Sample: Maps — village development
items.q: Two maps show a village in 2000 and today. (2000: farmland in north, forest in east, one road, small school. Today: housing estate replaced farmland, forest partly cleared for a car park, road widened, school extended, new supermarket in centre.)
items.html:
The maps compare the village of [Riverside] in 2000 and at present.

Overall, the village has become considerably more developed, with farmland and part of the forest making way for housing and new facilities.

In 2000, the north of the village was dominated by farmland, while a large forest covered the eastern side. A single road ran through the centre, and there was a small school to the west of it.

Today, the farmland in the north has been replaced by a housing estate, and part of the forest has been cleared to make way for a car park. The main road has been widened, and a supermarket has been built in the centre of the village. In addition, the school has been extended, presumably to accommodate the growing population.

sections.title: Speaking Part 1
sections.intro:
Formula: Direct answer → Reason → Example/detail (→ optional contrast). 2–4 sentences, ~20 seconds.

Examiners spot recited answers and mark them down. Learn the chunks and the shape, then say it in your own words with your own facts. [X] = your details.

items.title: Part 1 formula + openers
items.q: What is the Part 1 answer formula? Give 4 natural openers.
items.tip: Don't start every answer with "Yes, I do." Vary the first words.
items.html:
• Formula: Answer → Why → Example → (But / Though…)
  • To be honest, … · I'd say … · Actually, not really — … · It depends, really. …
  • Buying time: That's an interesting question — I've never really thought about it, but …
  • Extending: The main reason is that … · For instance, … · Having said that, …

items.title: Work or study
items.q: Do you work or are you a student?
items.html: I'm currently working as a [software developer] at a [small tech company]. What I enjoy most about it is solving problems, although the deadlines can be quite stressful. I'm also preparing for IELTS because I'm hoping to work abroad in the next couple of years.

items.title: Hometown
items.q: Tell me about your hometown.
items.html: I'm from [Pune], which is a fairly large city in [western India]. It's best known for its universities, so there's a really youthful atmosphere. The only downside is the traffic — it's got much worse in the last ten years as the city has grown.

items.title: Home
items.q: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
items.html: I live in a two-bedroom apartment on the fifth floor of a building near the city centre. It's not huge, but it's really convenient — I can walk to the shops and the metro. If I could change one thing, I'd love a balcony with a bit more space for plants.

items.title: Daily routine
items.q: What is your daily routine like?
items.html: On weekdays it's pretty predictable. I get up at about seven, grab a quick breakfast and start work by nine. Evenings are when I have a bit more freedom — I usually go for a walk or study English for an hour before winding down with a series.

items.title: Food & cooking
items.q: Do you like cooking?
items.html: I wouldn't call myself a great cook, but I do enjoy it, especially at weekends when I'm not in a rush. I mostly make simple dishes from my home region. I find it quite relaxing, and it's much healthier than ordering takeaway all the time.

items.title: Weather
items.q: What kind of weather do you like?
items.html: I'm a big fan of cool, dry weather, like early winter where I live. Intense heat really drains my energy, so summer isn't my favourite season. That said, I love the first rain of the monsoon — the smell of the earth is amazing.

items.title: Music
items.q: What kind of music do you listen to?
items.html: I've got quite eclectic taste, to be honest. I listen to old film songs with my parents, but on my own I'm more into indie and acoustic music. I usually have something playing in the background while I'm working — it helps me concentrate.

items.title: Reading
items.q: Do you enjoy reading?
items.html: Yes, though I don't read as much as I used to. These days I mostly read on my phone — articles and the occasional novel. I'd like to get back into reading paper books, because I find it easier to switch off without notifications popping up.

items.title: Sport & exercise
items.q: Do you do any sport?
items.html: Not competitively, but I try to stay active. I go jogging three or four times a week, usually early in the morning before it gets too hot. It's a great way to clear my head before work.

items.title: Travel
items.q: Do you like travelling?
items.html: Absolutely — I try to take at least one trip a year. I prefer places off the beaten track rather than big tourist cities, because they feel more authentic. Last year I went to [the mountains in the north], and it was the most peaceful week I've had in ages.

items.title: Phone & technology
items.q: How often do you use your phone?
items.html: Far more than I should, if I'm honest! I use it for everything — work messages, maps, banking. I've recently set a screen-time limit on social media apps, because I noticed I was mindlessly scrolling late at night.

items.title: Friends
items.q: Do you prefer to have a few close friends or many friends?
items.html: Definitely a few close friends. I'm fairly introverted, so I'd rather have deep conversations with two or three people than make small talk at a big party. Most of my close friends go back to my school days.

items.title: Shopping
items.q: Do you like shopping?
items.html: It depends on what I'm shopping for. I quite enjoy browsing in bookshops, but clothes shopping isn't really my thing — I usually know what I want and order it online to save time.

items.title: Weekends
items.q: What do you usually do at weekends?
items.html: I try to keep my weekends fairly relaxed. On Saturdays I catch up on chores and maybe meet friends for dinner, and Sundays are for recharging — a long breakfast with family and an afternoon nap.

items.title: Sleep
items.q: Do you get enough sleep?
items.html: Not always, unfortunately. When I have deadlines, I tend to stay up late and then feel sluggish the next day. I'm trying to stick to a regular bedtime, and putting my phone away an hour before bed has helped a lot.

items.title: Social media
items.q: Do you use social media much?
items.html: Less than I used to. I mainly use it to keep up with friends and follow a few accounts about language learning. I deleted a couple of apps last year because they were eating up too much of my time.

items.title: Learning English
items.q: Why are you learning English?
items.html: Mainly for my career. Most of the cutting-edge material in my field is in English, and I'm hoping to move abroad for work. Besides that, I genuinely enjoy films and podcasts in English, so it doesn't feel like a chore.

items.title: Films & TV
items.q: What kind of films do you like?
items.html: I'm really into thrillers and anything based on a true story. I like films that keep you guessing until the very end. I'm not a big fan of superhero films, though — they all feel a bit similar to me.

items.title: Public transport
items.q: Do you often use public transport?
items.html: Yes, almost every day. The metro in my city is quick and affordable, and it saves me the stress of driving in traffic. The only drawback is that it gets incredibly crowded during rush hour.

items.title: Celebrations
items.q: How do you usually celebrate your birthday?
items.html: Nothing too extravagant. I usually go out for a meal with my family or a few close friends. As I've got older, I've come to prefer quiet celebrations to big parties.

sections.title: Speaking Part 2
sections.intro:
1 minute to prepare, speak 2 minutes. Template: Intro → Background (when/where/who) → Details (cover every bullet) → Feelings → Why it matters / wrap-up.

Trick: prepare ~8 flexible stories. One story fits many cue cards (your grandfather = person you admire / old person / advice / skill someone taught you).

items.title: Part 2 template
items.q: Say the 5-step Part 2 template with one opener for each step.
items.tip: Use the 1-minute prep to write 5 keywords, one per step — not sentences.
items.html:
• Intro: I'd like to talk about [X], which/who …
  • Background: This was back in [year], when I was … · I first met him when …
  • Details: What stands out most is that … · The thing I remember most clearly is …
  • Feelings: I have to say I was [absolutely thrilled / quite nervous] … · It made me realise that …
  • Wrap-up: Looking back, it was [a turning point] … · That's why it means so much to me.

items.title: Person you admire
items.q: Describe a person you admire. Say who this person is, how you know them, what they have done, and explain why you admire them.
items.tip: Also fits: an old person you know · someone who gave you advice · a family member you are close to · someone who taught you a skill.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about my grandfather, who is without doubt the person I admire most. He grew up in a small village with very little money, and he had to leave school at fourteen to support his family by working on a farm.

What stands out most about him is his determination. Even though he had no formal qualifications, he taught himself accounting in the evenings and eventually set up his own small business selling agricultural equipment. By the time he retired, he had paid for all four of his children to go to university — something he had never had the chance to do himself.

I spent a lot of time with him when I was a child, and the thing I remember most clearly is that he never complained. Whenever I was going through a difficult time at school, he would tell me stories about his early life and remind me that setbacks are only temporary.

I admire him because he proves that background doesn't determine your future. Whenever I feel like giving up — including while preparing for this exam, actually — I think of him. That's why he means so much to me.

items.title: Place you'd like to visit
items.q: Describe a place you would like to visit. Say where it is, how you know about it, what you would do there, and explain why you want to go.
items.tip: Also fits: a city you'd like to live in · a beautiful natural place · a holiday you'd like to take.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about Iceland, which has been at the top of my travel list for years. I first came across it in a documentary about the Northern Lights, and the images completely blew me away.

If I went, I'd hire a car and drive along the ring road that circles the island. I'd love to see the glaciers, the black-sand beaches and the waterfalls, and of course I'd stay up at night hoping to see the aurora. I've also read that you can bathe in natural hot springs outdoors even when it's snowing, which sounds like a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

The main reason I want to go is that it's so different from where I live. My city is hot, crowded and noisy, whereas Iceland seems wild, empty and peaceful. I think spending time in a place like that would give me a real sense of perspective.

The only thing holding me back is the cost — it's one of the most expensive countries in the world — so I'm saving up and hoping to go in the next few years.

items.title: Useful object / gadget
items.q: Describe a piece of technology (or object) you find useful. Say what it is, when you got it, how you use it, and explain why it is useful.
items.tip: Also fits: something you bought recently · a gift you received · something you can't live without.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about my noise-cancelling headphones, which have made a huge difference to my daily life. I bought them about two years ago, when I started commuting by metro, after reading countless reviews online.

I use them pretty much every day. On the train they block out the noise completely, so I can listen to podcasts — mostly English ones, as part of my IELTS preparation. At home, I wear them when I need to concentrate, because my street can be quite loud.

To be honest, I was a bit reluctant to buy them at first, because they weren't cheap. But I've definitely got my money's worth. The battery lasts for days, and they're comfortable enough to wear for hours.

The main reason they're so useful is that they give me a bit of personal space in a crowded city. Without them, my commute would be exhausting; with them, it's become the most productive part of my day.

items.title: Book or film you enjoyed
items.q: Describe a book you enjoyed reading. Say what it was, when you read it, what it was about, and explain why you enjoyed it.
items.tip: Also fits: a film that made an impression · a story you heard · something you learned from the internet.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about a book called *Sapiens* by Yuval Noah Harari, which I read a couple of years ago on a long train journey.

It's a short history of humankind, from the first humans in Africa to the modern world. What makes it special is that it doesn't just list events; it asks big questions, like why humans came to dominate the planet and whether we're actually happier than our ancestors.

The thing I remember most clearly is the idea that humans cooperate on a huge scale because we believe in shared stories — things like money, nations and companies, which only exist because we all agree they do. That completely changed the way I think about everyday life.

I enjoyed it because it was thought-provoking but easy to read. The writing is clear, with lots of humour and examples. I've recommended it to several friends since, and I'd love to re-read it in a few years to see whether I still see things the same way.

items.title: Memorable journey
items.q: Describe a journey you remember well. Say where you went, how you travelled, who you went with, and explain why you remember it.
items.tip: Also fits: a time you got lost · a holiday you enjoyed · a time something went wrong · a time you were late.
items.html:
I'd like to describe a train journey I took from Mumbai to Goa with three close friends about five years ago, just after we'd finished university.

We'd planned to fly, but at the last minute the flights became too expensive, so we booked an overnight train instead. To be honest, I wasn't looking forward to it — twelve hours in a crowded carriage didn't sound much fun.

But it turned out to be the highlight of the trip. The route goes along the coast through the Western Ghats, and because it was the monsoon season, everything was incredibly green, with waterfalls pouring down the hills right next to the track. We sat by the open door for hours, chatting and drinking tea from vendors on the platforms.

I remember it so well because it was the last trip we all took together before we moved to different cities for work. It taught me that the journey can be more memorable than the destination, and now I deliberately choose trains whenever I can.

items.title: Time you helped someone
items.q: Describe a time you helped someone. Say who you helped, how you helped them, why you helped them, and explain how you felt about it.
items.tip: Also fits: a time you taught someone something · a good deed · a time you were proud of yourself.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about a time I helped my neighbour, an elderly woman who lives alone, learn to use a smartphone. This was during the pandemic, when she couldn't leave home and was feeling really cut off from her family.

Her son had sent her a phone, but she had no idea how to use it and was too embarrassed to ask. When I found out, I offered to help. I went round every evening for about a week, and we started with the absolute basics — answering calls, then sending messages, and finally making video calls.

It wasn't always easy. She would forget steps, so I wrote simple instructions on cards with big letters. The breakthrough came when she video-called her grandchildren for the first time — she was so happy she actually cried.

I felt incredibly proud, not because it was difficult for me, but because such a small thing made such a big difference to her. It also taught me a lot about patience. We still chat on the stairs, and she now sends me jokes on WhatsApp!

items.title: Skill you want to learn
items.q: Describe a skill you would like to learn. Say what it is, how you would learn it, why you want to learn it, and explain how it would help you.
items.tip: Also fits: a hobby you'd like to take up · something you'd like to be good at · a goal you have.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about learning to swim properly, which is something I've been meaning to do for years. I can just about stay afloat, but I can't swim more than a few metres without panicking.

I'd learn by signing up for adult classes at the sports centre near my home. I've heard the instructors are very patient with beginners, which is important because, to be completely honest, I'm a bit afraid of deep water after a bad experience as a child.

There are a few reasons I want to learn. Firstly, it's a matter of safety — if I ever fell into water, I'd be in serious trouble. Secondly, swimming is one of the best forms of exercise, and it's easy on the joints. And finally, I'd love to be able to enjoy beach holidays instead of just sitting on the sand.

I think it would help me overcome a long-standing fear, and that kind of success often gives you confidence in other areas of life too.

items.title: Website or app
items.q: Describe a website or app you use often. Say what it is, how you found it, what you use it for, and explain why you like it.
items.tip: Also fits: a piece of technology · something that helps you study · a way you relax.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about YouTube, which I use almost every single day. I can't remember exactly when I started, but it was probably in school, for help with maths homework.

These days I use it mainly for two things. Firstly, for learning — I watch IELTS lessons, coding tutorials and documentaries. Secondly, for unwinding in the evenings — I follow a few travel and cooking channels.

What I like most is that you can learn almost anything for free. When my laptop broke last year, I managed to fix it myself by following a video, which saved me quite a lot of money. I also like that I can slow videos down and turn on subtitles, which is great for my English.

The downside is that it can be addictive — the recommendations are so good that one video easily turns into ten. So I've started using it more deliberately, only watching things I've saved in a list.

items.title: Festival or celebration
items.q: Describe a festival or celebration that is important in your country. Say what it is, when it happens, what people do, and explain why it is important.
items.tip: Also fits: a family event · a wedding you went to · a special day · a time you were happy.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about Diwali, the festival of lights, which is one of the most important festivals in India. It usually takes place in October or November and lasts for about five days.

In the run-up to the festival, people clean and decorate their homes, and buy new clothes and sweets. On the main night, every house is lit up with small oil lamps and fairy lights, and families gather to pray, exchange gifts and share an enormous meal. Later, there are fireworks — although many cities have cracked down on them recently because of air pollution.

For me, the best part is the sense of togetherness. My relatives travel from different cities, so it's often the only time of year we're all under one roof.

It's important because it symbolises the victory of light over darkness, and of good over evil. Beyond the religious meaning, it's a chance to reconnect with family and leave the past year behind.

items.title: Important decision
items.q: Describe an important decision you made. Say what the decision was, when you made it, how you made it, and explain why it was important.
items.tip: Also fits: a change in your life · a goal you achieved · a time you were brave · a plan for the future.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about my decision to change career, which I made about three years ago.

At the time, I was working in sales. It was well paid, but I wasn't finding it fulfilling at all, and I'd started to dread Monday mornings. I'd always been interested in computers, so I began teaching myself programming in the evenings.

The decision wasn't easy. I spent months weighing up the pros and cons. My parents were worried, since I'd be giving up a stable salary. In the end, I made a list of what I wanted in five years' time, and it became obvious that staying wasn't an option. I did a six-month course, and it paid off — I got my first developer job soon after.

It was important because it taught me that it's never too late to change direction. I earn a bit less than before, but I'm far more motivated, and it's actually the reason I'm taking IELTS — I'd like to work abroad in tech.

items.title: Advice you received
items.q: Describe a piece of good advice you received. Say who gave it, when you received it, what it was, and explain why it was useful.
items.tip: Also fits: a person who influenced you · a teacher you remember · something you learned from an older person.
items.html:
I'd like to talk about a piece of advice my first manager gave me: "Done is better than perfect."

This was in my first year of work. I was given a report to write and spent so long trying to make it perfect that I missed the deadline. Instead of getting angry, my manager took me aside and explained that a good piece of work delivered on time is far more valuable than a perfect one delivered late.

At first, I found it hard to accept, because I'd always been a perfectionist. But I started applying it — setting myself time limits and getting feedback early instead of polishing things for hours.

It was useful because it reduced my stress enormously and made me more productive. I use it even now with IELTS writing: rather than aiming for a flawless essay, I make sure I finish both tasks in the time. It's simple, but it's changed the way I work.

sections.title: Speaking Part 3
sections.intro:
Abstract questions about society. Formula: Answer (opinion) → Reason → Example → Contrast / future ("ARE+"). 30–45 seconds.

Talk about people in general, not only yourself. Topic Bank ideas (deck 2) work here too.

items.title: Part 3 formula
items.q: What is the Part 3 answer formula? Give one phrase for each step.
items.html:
• Answer: I'd say that, on the whole, … · I'm fairly convinced that …
  • Reason: The main reason for this is that … · This is largely because …
  • Example: Take [my country], for example. … · A good example of this is …
  • Contrast / future: Having said that, … · I suspect that in the future …

items.title: Phrases: buying time & unknown topics
items.q: You don't know much about the topic. Give 4 phrases that buy time naturally.
items.html:
• That's a tricky one to answer, but …
  • I've never really considered that before, but I suppose …
  • I'm not an expert on this, but my impression is that …
  • Off the top of my head, I'd say …

items.title: Phrases: speculating & comparing
items.q: Give 4 phrases for speculating about the future and 4 for comparing past and present.
items.html:
• Future: It seems likely that … · There's a good chance that … · I wouldn't be surprised if … · In all likelihood, …
  • Past vs now: Back in my parents' day, … · These days, by contrast, … · Compared with a generation ago, … · Things have changed beyond recognition.

items.title: Phrases: balanced & conceding
items.q: Give 4 phrases to show both sides / partly agree.
items.html:
• It's a double-edged sword. …
  • There are pros and cons. On the plus side, … but on the downside, …
  • I can see where people are coming from, but …
  • To some extent, yes, but …

items.title: Education
items.q: Do you think the role of teachers will change in the future because of technology?
items.html: I'd say it's already changing. The main reason is that information is now freely available online, so teachers no longer need to be the main source of knowledge. Instead, they're becoming more like coaches — helping students make sense of information and think critically. Take online courses, for example: they can explain a concept perfectly well, but they can't notice when a student is struggling or losing motivation. So I suspect that teachers will become more important, not less, just in a different way.

items.title: Technology
items.q: Has technology made people less social?
items.html: It's a double-edged sword. On the one hand, people spend hours on their phones even when they're with friends, which I think damages the quality of face-to-face conversation. On the other hand, technology helps people stay connected who would otherwise be isolated — elderly people talking to their grandchildren abroad, for instance. So I'd say it hasn't made us less social overall; it's changed the way we socialise.

items.title: Environment
items.q: Whose responsibility is it to protect the environment — individuals or governments?
items.html: I'm fairly convinced that governments have to take the lead, simply because individual actions can only go so far. I can recycle and avoid plastic, but that's a drop in the ocean compared with the emissions from a single power station. Governments can pass laws, set targets and invest in renewable energy. Having said that, individuals still matter, because politicians tend to act on what voters care about.

items.title: Work
items.q: Why do some people prefer to be self-employed?
items.html: The main attraction is independence. Self-employed people can choose their own hours, decide which projects to take on, and they don't have to answer to a boss. A good example is the huge growth in freelance designers and developers, who can work for clients all over the world from home. The flip side, of course, is the lack of a steady income — there's no sick pay or pension, which is why many people find it too risky.

items.title: Cities
items.q: Why do so many people move from the countryside to cities?
items.html: It mainly comes down to jobs and opportunities. Cities offer far more employment options, especially for educated young people, as well as better hospitals and universities. In my country, for instance, millions of people have moved to major cities over the last twenty years. The problem is that cities often can't keep up with the population growth, which leads to overcrowding, traffic and sky-high rents.

items.title: Family
items.q: How has family life changed compared with the past?
items.html: Things have changed beyond recognition, really. Back in my grandparents' day, three generations would often live under one roof, whereas these days most young couples live separately. Families are also smaller, and in many homes both parents work. I think the biggest change is that families spend less time together — everyone's busy, and meals in front of screens have replaced long conversations at the dinner table.

items.title: Health
items.q: Why do you think many people don't exercise enough?
items.html: I'd put it down to modern lifestyles. Most people sit at a desk all day, commute by car or bus, and by the evening they're too exhausted to work out. On top of that, gyms can be expensive, and in big cities there aren't always safe places to walk or run. I think the solution is to build exercise into daily life — cycling to work, taking the stairs — rather than relying on willpower.

items.title: Media
items.q: Do you think people trust the news less than in the past?
items.html: Yes, I think there's been a definite decline. This is largely because of social media, where anyone can publish anything, so people have become used to seeing false stories. On top of that, many news outlets are seen as politically biased. The worrying thing is that when people stop trusting reliable sources, they often turn to even less reliable ones.

items.title: Tourism
items.q: What are the negative effects of tourism on local people?
items.html: The most obvious one is rising costs. In popular destinations, landlords rent out flats to tourists, which pushes up rents for local families. Take Barcelona for example — many residents have had to move out of the city centre. There's also the issue of overcrowding: it can be difficult to go about your daily life when your street is full of tour groups.

items.title: Shopping & consumerism
items.q: Why do people buy things they don't need?
items.html: I think advertising plays a huge role. Companies are extremely skilled at making us feel that a new phone or new clothes will make us happier. Social media has made this even worse, because people are constantly comparing themselves to others. Having said that, I've noticed that more young people are turning to second-hand shopping and minimalism, so the tide may be turning.

items.title: Sport
items.q: Should sport be compulsory in schools?
items.html: Yes, I strongly believe it should be. Childhood obesity is on the rise, and for many children, school PE is the only regular exercise they get. Sport also teaches valuable life skills like teamwork and dealing with defeat. That said, schools should offer a wide range of activities — not everyone enjoys football, but they might love dance or yoga.

items.title: Ageing population
items.q: What problems might an ageing population cause?
items.html: The biggest concern is the cost. As the proportion of older people grows, there are fewer working-age people paying taxes to fund pensions and healthcare. Japan is a good example — it's facing a serious labour shortage and has had to rely more on robots and immigration. I suspect that many countries will have to raise the retirement age in the coming decades.

items.title: Science
items.q: Is it worth spending money on space exploration?
items.html: To some extent, yes. Space research has given us technologies we take for granted, like GPS and accurate weather forecasts. It also inspires young people to study science. Having said that, I can see why people feel uneasy when there's so much poverty on Earth. Personally, I think the best approach is for private companies to take on more of the cost, so that public money goes to more urgent problems.
